chapter: Early years: Cleveland, Aaronson, New York
title: Bix and Louis as two ends of jazz; Whitney Balliett on Lester Young
summary: He contrasts Louis as black and Bix as white jazz and objects to Balliett dismissing Trumbauer and Jimmy Dorsey as Lester Young's influences.

story.theme_name: Lester Young: the man, the sound, the Basie years
story.community_name: Remembering Lester Young: Prez the man and his sound

blocks.x: But both of them jazz. Both of them playing unmistakable jazz. Louis’s was black, and his was white. When I first heard Louis, after having been indoctrinated by Bix—Bix and [Frankie] Trumbauer . . . Interesting, because I read something Whitney Balliett wrote in a piece on Lester Young. Les was my idea of a consumate jazz musician. A “musician,” is the word. He said that when he asked Lester—and I knew this—who were his influences, he said Tram [Frankie Trumbauer] and Jimmy Dorsey. And Whitney says both of whom . . . neither of whom were good jazz players. Well they were the only jazz players there were at that instrument at that time. I don’t know what he’s talking about. I get so bored with these didactic olympian sayings . . . statements these guys make. Whitney’s a good writer, but it’s an enormous prejudice to say these guys weren’t good jazz players. In their day, they were the only jazz players on those instruments.
And you were there and he wasn’t.
You were there and he wasn’t.
